catalog_quote: Les fait de prosodie englobent l’accent tonique, prévisible et donc non distinctif, ainsi que la hauteur tonale, distinctive dans le lexique nominal ... Les règles de placement de l’accent tonique sont identiques dans le système nominal et le système verbal. La position de l’accent est déterminée à la fois par la hauteur tonale – une syllabe portant un ton haut étant systématiquement accentuée, la longueur vocalique – une voyelle longue, quelle que soit la hauteur tonale, étant elle aussi accentuée, et la structure syllabique du mot – la première syllabe d’un trisyllabe dont la dernière syllabe est accentuée étant accentuée, même lorsque les conditions de longueur vocalique et de hauteur tonale ne sont pas remplies. ... Dans un mot constitué d’une séquence de syllabes comprenant des voyelles brèves et des ton bas, ces syllabes sont de même poids, et porteront toutes un accent tonique, d…

tone_statements.citation: Blench, Roger. 2021. The Maban languages and their place within Nilo-Saharan. Unpublished paper circulated on Academia.edu (item 44876227).
tone_statements.quote: 4.3 Tones Lukas (1953) and Caprile (1977) both mark tones and Weiss (2009) concludes that a system of High, Low, Rising and Falling can be established for Maba, albeit the contrast with glide tones only occurs in rather specific contexts. Nougayrol (1989) recognises two tone heights for Aiki, and does not mention glide tones.
tone_statements.summary: Survey crediting Weiss 2009: High, Low, Rising, Falling; the glide (contour) contrast arises only in specific contexts. No TBU, downstep or stress discussed; Appendix I Maba forms are tone-marked.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both the deciding passage (sec. 2.2-2.2.1, pp. 43-45) and the weight definition (sec. 2.3.2.2, pp. 58-59) are verbatim in the text-layer PDF we hold/txt of Weiss 2009 at the stated locators. (2) Deciding source: a 2009 Lyon-2 doctoral thesis that functions as the reference grammar of Maba (Glottolog's sole 'grammar', 480 pp), with an explicit, example-supported statement that stress is predictable, non-distinctive, assigned to every heavy syllable (heavy = long V or H tone; CVC light), plus rhythmic initial stress in trisyllables with final stress and all-syllable stress in all-light words — exactly what the catalog's 'weight', non-strict, unbounded, what counts as heavy/heavy fields encode. (3) Alternatives: Glottolog's full descriptive list (9 items) contains nothing newer or more phonological; HAL returns only this thesis for the author and for maba+phonology; StressTyp2 has no Maba rec

sources.note: The work is a comparative vocabulary with a grammatical introduction. Its only statements about accent are general, for all nine languages: Barth marks vowels as short, long by origin (macron) or bearing a 'moveable accent' (acute), and claims a consistent accent system. The Maba chapter (pronouns, verb, noun, gender, adjectives, monosyllabic roots, comparison with Fur/Kanuri/Bagirmi) states no stress rule, no secondary stress, no weight condition, no domain and no tone for Maba. sources.note: This work describes Fur / Darfour or Wadai (the work treats 'Fur, Darfour or Wadai' as one idiom; only a 10-item numerals list, no prosodic remark). The one stress remark in the book is about Massina (Foulah/Fellatah), from an informant. Wadai appears only as a label conflated with Darfur/Fur; the section gives a numerals list (Seda 1, Wosin 2, Sebda 3, Seksa 4, Oogoo 5, Sebsa 6, Tieska 7, Korsa 8, Biskina 9, Engoda 10) and no statement on stress, accent or tone. Nothing bears on the catalog entry (Weiss 2009 weight rule).

sources.citation: Abū Naẓīfa, ʿAbd Allāh Muḥammad Aḥmad. 2012. Tajribat kitābat lughat al-Mabā bi-l-ḥarf al-Qurʾānī al-munammaṭ [تجربة كتابة لغة المبا بالحرف القرآني المنمط / An experiment in writing the Maba language in standardized Quranic script]. Paper posted on the blog BARGOU MABAA, 1 March 2012.
sources.tag: read: notes on tone
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request)
sources.note: An Arabic-script (Quranic-letter) orthography proposal: identifies the Maba sounds and their points of articulation, adds eleven letters for sounds absent from Arabic, uses the three Arabic vowel signs and sukun; words are written 'phonetically/prosodically as pronounced'. Prosody appears only once: diacritics (a dot, dash or mark) may be needed 'to indicate an accent (nabra) or imala'. No tone inventory, no tone marking convention, no statement that pitch is distinctive.
sources.venue: Paper posted on the blog BARGOU MABAA, 1 March 2012

tone.quote: فمن أجل ذلك كله نكتب كلمات برامبا ( لغة المبا – الوداى ) كتابة صوتية عروضية أي نكتب ما ينطق فقط من الكلمة وما يسمع منها حين النطق بها ، ولا نزيد عليه ولا ننقصه . وقد نحتاج إلى نقطة أو شرطة أو علامة لتمييز حرف من الآخر ، أو لبيان نبرة أو إمالة ، لتوضع فوق الحرف أو تحته أو فيه
tone.translation: For all these reasons we write the words of Bura Maba (the Maba language, Wadai) in a phonetic, prosodic spelling, i.e. we write only what is pronounced of the word and what is heard when it is uttered, adding nothing and omitting nothing. We may need a dot, a dash or a mark to distinguish one letter from another, or to indicate an accent (nabra) or a vowel inclination (imala), to be placed above, below or inside the letter.
tone.summary: None given (accent/'nabra' mentioned as something a diacritic might mark; tone not discussed).
tone.says: An Arabic-script (Quranic-letter) orthography proposal: identifies the Maba sounds and their points of articulation, adds eleven letters for sounds absent from Arabic, uses the three Arabic vowel signs and sukun; words are written 'phonetically/prosodically as pronounced'. Prosody appears only once: diacritics (a dot, dash or mark) may be needed 'to indicate an accent (nabra) or imala'. No tone inventory, no tone marking convention, no statement that pitch is distinctive.
